title: The king and the handmaid
hook: a king loves a young woman who falls ill, and no doctor can help (Masnavi 1.36ff)

segments.voice: Last week closed with providence: Marcus thanking the gods for all he never earned. Your line was this happened to me, and I didn't arrange it.

Tired, so more coffee. Unhappy at work, so more hours. Lonely, so another app. Sometimes the fix becomes the problem, and each round makes things a little worse. Rumi's first story in the Masnavi starts right there. A king out hunting sees a young woman, a servant girl, and falls in love. He buys her and brings her home. Almost at once she falls ill, and she keeps getting worse. Today, the king and the handmaid.
screen: `TRYING HARDER, GETTING WORSE.` → `A KING SEES A YOUNG WOMAN.` → `THE KING AND THE HANDMAID.`

segments.voice: First, the setting, honestly. In Rumi's world a king could buy a servant girl, and the story takes that for granted. It's hard to hear today, and it's fine to feel that. Rumi tells it as a parable about the soul, not a model of love. The king gathers the best physicians from everywhere: save her, and I'll give you anything. They're confident. Each of us, they say, has a cure for every pain; we'll heal her. And Rumi notices something. Out of pride, they don't say, if God wills. It sounds tiny, but behind it stands a verse of the Quran, in Pickthall's translation: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." Rumi doesn't mean just saying the words. He means the humility inside them: knowing the outcome isn't fully yours. The physicians try remedy after remedy, and every cure does the opposite of what it should. The girl grows thin as a hair. The king weeps. Finally he sees it: this isn't working. He runs barefoot to the mosque, weeps on the prayer mat until it's wet, and prays for help. The answer is tomorrow's story. The physicians weren't bad at medicine. They were sure of themselves, and they were treating the wrong illness. Sometimes the honest first step is the king's plain admission: it isn't working.
screen: `A KING BUYS A SERVANT GIRL.` · `THE PHYSICIANS FORGET: IF GOD WILLS.` · `EVERY CURE MAKES IT WORSE.` · `BAREFOOT TO THE MOSQUE.` · then, large: `IT ISN'T WORKING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you keep doing to feel better that doesn't really help: scrolling to calm down, working late to feel safe, snacking when you're lonely, staying busy so you won't feel sad. Don't scold yourself; just see it clearly, the way the king finally did, and say inside: it isn't working. Then sit quietly with not knowing what would.
Masnavi, Rumi's book of stories: its first tale, where proud physicians' cures only make the dying girl worse. Today's word.
Your line: it isn't working. The king is still on the prayer mat, and the story isn't over. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 171 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PHYSICIAN FROM THE UNSEEN.`

howItsDone: The story of the king and the handmaid is the first tale of the Masnavi, and Sufi teachers traditionally read it as an allegory of the soul, its false loves and its true healer.
